claim: Learning invariances allows us to generalise.
source: Learning invariances allows us to generalise.
evidence: This is a general statement about learning and generalization that draws from established scientific understanding.

claim: Invariant representations in the visual modality allow us to recognise objects despite translations or rotations in physical space.
source: In the visual modality, invariant representations allow us to recognise objects despite translations or rotations in physical space.
evidence: This statement reflects established knowledge in vision science about object recognition.

claim: Humans naturally generalise to rotated exemplars when stimuli are defined in physical space.
source: We find that humans naturally generalise to rotated exemplars when stimuli are defined in physical space, but not when they are defined as positions on a nonspatial feature manifold.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the study comparing spatial and nonspatial conditions.

claim: Humans do not naturally generalise to rotated exemplars when stimuli are defined as positions on a nonspatial feature manifold.
source: We find that humans naturally generalise to rotated exemplars when stimuli are defined in physical space, but not when they are defined as positions on a nonspatial feature manifold.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the study comparing spatial and nonspatial conditions.

claim: If participants are first pre-trained to map auditory or visual features to spatial locations, then rotational generalisation becomes possible even in nonspatial domains.
source: However, if participants are first pre-trained to map auditory or visual features to spatial locations, then rotational generalisation becomes possible even in nonspatial domains.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from Experiments 2 and 3 showing the effect of spatial pre-training.

claim: Space acts as a scaffold for learning more abstract conceptual invariances.
source: These results imply that space acts as a scaffold for learning more abstract conceptual invariances.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results showing the effect of spatial pre-training on nonspatial generalization.

claim: Humans form mental representations that are invariant to transformation to recognise objects and events in the natural world.
source: To recognise objects and events in the natural world, humans form mental representations that are invariant to transformation.
evidence: This statement reflects established knowledge in cognitive science about object recognition.

claim: The existence of invariant representations allows entities to be recognised and categorised despite changes in their surface properties, which is called 'generalisation'.
source: The existence of invariant representations allows entities to be recognised and categorised despite changes in their surface properties, which is called 'generalisation'.
evidence: This is a definitional statement about generalization in cognitive science.

claim: The formation of invariances has been most extensively studied in the case of visual object recognition.
source: The formation of invariances has been most extensively studied in the case of visual object recognition.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of research in the field.

claim: We have no trouble recognising a teapot that is moved to a new location (translated), tipped on its side (rotated) or viewed from afar (rescaled).
source: For example, we have no trouble recognising a teapot that is moved to a new location (translated), tipped on its side (rotated) or viewed from afar (rescaled).
evidence: This is an example illustrating a well-known phenomenon in visual object recognition.

claim: Theories about how we recognise transformed objects are based on assembly from geometric primitives.
source: How we do so has provoked diverse theories based on assembly from geometric primitives (Biederman, 1987; Marr, 1982), associative learning (Rock and DiVita, 1987; Wallis and Bülthoff, 1999), and function approximation in deep networks (Lindsay, 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work in the field.

claim: Theories about how we recognise transformed objects are based on associative learning.
source: How we do so has provoked diverse theories based on assembly from geometric primitives (Biederman, 1987; Marr, 1982), associative learning (Rock and DiVita, 1987; Wallis and Bülthoff, 1999), and function approximation in deep networks (Lindsay, 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work in the field.

claim: Theories about how we recognise transformed objects are based on function approximation in deep networks.
source: How we do so has provoked diverse theories based on assembly from geometric primitives (Biederman, 1987; Marr, 1982), associative learning (Rock and DiVita, 1987; Wallis and Bülthoff, 1999), and function approximation in deep networks (Lindsay, 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work in the field.

claim: The concept of a 'tree' implies an entity whose structure is defined by a nested hierarchy.
source: For example, the concept of a 'tree' implies an entity whose structure is defined by a nested hierarchy, whether this is a physical object whose parts are arranged in space (such as an oak tree in a forest) or a more abstract data structure (such as a family tree or taxonomic tree).
evidence: This is an example illustrating abstract conceptual structure.

claim: The concept of a 'ring' implies an entity whose features are arranged cyclically.
source: The concept of a 'ring' implies an entity whose features are arranged cyclically, whether a physical ring (worn on the finger), the (circular) temporal pattern of tones in a peal of bells, or the periodicity in the passage of the seasons (Kemp and Tenenbaum, 2008).
evidence: This is an example illustrating abstract conceptual structure, with citation to prior work.

claim: Humans perceive oak trees, family trees, and taxonomic trees as different instances of a more abstract concept defined by the same relational structure despite great changes in their surface properties.
source: Despite great changes in the surface properties of oak trees, family trees, and taxonomic trees, humans perceive them as different instances of a more abstract concept defined by the same relational structure.
evidence: This is a statement about human conceptual abilities that reflects established knowledge.

claim: The human ability to readily form invariances over abstract concepts remains a puzzle for cognitive and neural scientists.
source: The human ability to readily form invariances over abstract concepts remains a puzzle for both cognitive and neural scientists hoping to understand neural computations, and a challenge for AI researchers wishing to build intelligent agents.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of understanding in the field.

claim: One prominent theory argues that we learn invariant concepts because of the way the brain represents physical space.
source: One prominent theory argues that we learn invariant concepts because of the way the brain represents physical space (Behrens et al., 2018; Bellmund et al., 2018; Summerfield et al., 2020; Gärdenfors, 2000; Tversky, 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior theoretical work.

claim: Neurons coding for positions in either egocentric or allocentric space can be recycled to represent locations in more abstract spaces defined by continuous variation in features.
source: This argument states that neurons coding for positions in either egocentric (viewer-centred) or allocentric (world-centred) space can be recycled to represent locations in more abstract spaces, defined by continuous variation in features (e.g. red to blue, quiet to loud).
evidence: This is a theoretical claim about neural representation.

claim: This theory is backed up by proof-of-concept computational simulations.
source: This theory is backed up by proof-of-concept computational simulations (Whittington et al., 2020), and by findings that brain regions thought to be critical for spatial cognition in mammals (such as the hippocampal-entorhinal complex and parietal cortex) exhibit neural codes that are invariant to relational transformations of nonspatial stimuli (Park et al., 2021; Park et al., 2020; Mack et al., 2018; Constantinescu et al., 2016; Viganò and Piazza, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to computational modeling work.

claim: Brain regions thought to be critical for spatial cognition in mammals exhibit neural codes that are invariant to relational transformations of nonspatial stimuli.
source: This theory is backed up by proof-of-concept computational simulations (Whittington et al., 2020), and by findings that brain regions thought to be critical for spatial cognition in mammals (such as the hippocampal-entorhinal complex and parietal cortex) exhibit neural codes that are invariant to relational transformations of nonspatial stimuli (Park et al., 2021; Park et al., 2020; Mack et al., 2018; Constantinescu et al., 2016; Viganò and Piazza, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to empirical neuroscience studies.

claim: The theory that learning about physical space scaffolds conceptual generalisation lacks direct empirical evidence.
source: However, whilst promising, this theory lacks direct empirical evidence.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of evidence for a theory.

claim: Participants made category judgments about a sequence of four successive stimuli in either auditory, visual, or spatial modalities.
source: In the four studies described here, participants made category judgments about a sequence of four successive stimuli in either auditory, visual, or spatial modalities.
evidence: This describes the experimental design of the study.

claim: In auditory and visual modalities, the stimulus was drawn from a two-dimensional (2D) feature manifold.
source: In auditory and visual modalities, the stimulus was drawn from a two-dimensional (2D) feature manifold (e.g. a bivariate 'space' defined by colour and shape in the visual modality or pitch and timbre in the auditory modality).
evidence: This describes the experimental design of the study.

claim: Concepts were defined by a common pattern of transitions through either feature space or physical space.
source: Concepts were defined by a common pattern of transitions through either feature space or physical space.
evidence: This describes the experimental design of the study.

claim: There is already good evidence that nonspatial concepts are represented in a translation-invariant format.
source: There is already good evidence that nonspatial concepts are represented in a translation-invariant format.
evidence: This is a statement about existing evidence in the field.

claim: In the auditory domain, we can recognise 'auditory objects' that are translated in feature space.
source: For example, in the auditory domain, we can recognise 'auditory objects' that are translated in feature space (e.g. pitch and timbre). This occurs when we understand the same sentence from different speakers, or identify the same melody played with different musical instruments (Winkler et al., 2009; Griffiths and Warren, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work and common knowledge about auditory perception.

claim: Much less is known about the learning of rotational invariances for abstract concepts.
source: However, much less is known about the learning of rotational invariances for abstract concepts.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: In physical space, we readily learn rotation-invariant object representations.
source: In physical space, we readily learn rotation-invariant object representations (allowing us to recognise an upside-down teapot), and the computational mechanisms by which we do so have been a major fulcrum of debate in the vision sciences (Rock and DiVita, 1987; Wallis and Bülthoff, 1999).
evidence: This is a statement about established knowledge in vision science, supported by citations.

claim: Whether participants can learn rotationally invariant concepts in nonspatial domains is not known.
source: But whether participants can learn rotationally invariant concepts in nonspatial domains, i.e., those that are defined by sequences of visual and auditory features (rather than by locations in physical space, defined in Cartesian or polar coordinates) is not known.
evidence: This is a statement about the gap in knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: Participants cannot learn rotationally invariant concepts in nonspatial domains naively.
source: In the current study, we first test this, and find that naively, they cannot.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from Experiment 1.

claim: Teaching participants to map nonspatial features to spatial locations allows the learning of rotational invariances, even in nonspatial modalities.
source: Next, turning to our main hypothesis, we then ask if first teaching participants to map nonspatial features to spatial locations (providing a spatial scaffold) allows the learning of rotational invariances, even in nonspatial modalities. We find that it does.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from Experiments 2 and 3.

claim: A form of generalisation that is not usually possible for humans becomes possible when their understanding of the concept is 'scaffolded' by first learning a corresponding spatial representation.
source: This shows that a form of generalisation that is not usually possible for humans becomes possible when their understanding of the concept is 'scaffolded' by first learning a corresponding spatial representation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results.

claim: Abstract concept learning is linked to our understanding of physical space.
source: This thus supports the theory that abstract concept learning is linked to our understanding of physical space.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results supporting a theoretical claim.

claim: Participants learned the task well in all three conditions (auditory, visual, and spatial) in Experiment 1.
source: Participants learned the task well in all three conditions (but better in the spatial modality: intercept β=2.90 ± 0.19, slope associated with the auditory modality β=–1.91 ± 0.27, p<0.001, slope associated with the visual modality, β=–1.57 ± 0.26, p<0.001, mixed logistic regression on the probability of a correct response with participants as random effect).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of training data.

claim: Participants learned the task better in the spatial modality than in the auditory or visual modalities in Experiment 1.
source: Participants learned the task well in all three conditions (but better in the spatial modality: intercept β=2.90 ± 0.19, slope associated with the auditory modality β=–1.91 ± 0.27, p<0.001, slope associated with the visual modality, β=–1.57 ± 0.26, p<0.001, mixed logistic regression on the probability of a correct response with participants as random effect).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of training data.

claim: For near transfer in Experiment 1, all non-random participants in the auditory modality (26/26) learned a 1Du strategy.
source: For near transfer, all non-random participants in the auditory and visual modality (26/26 and 38/38) learned a 1Du strategy, whereas the vast majority in the spatial modality (35/41) were best fit by a 2D strategy.
evidence: This claim is supported by model fitting analysis of transfer data.

claim: For near transfer in Experiment 1, all non-random participants in the visual modality (38/38) learned a 1Du strategy.
source: For near transfer, all non-random participants in the auditory and visual modality (26/26 and 38/38) learned a 1Du strategy, whereas the vast majority in the spatial modality (35/41) were best fit by a 2D strategy.
evidence: This claim is supported by model fitting analysis of transfer data.

claim: For near transfer in Experiment 1, the vast majority of non-random participants in the spatial modality (35/41) were best fit by a 2D strategy.
source: For near transfer, all non-random participants in the auditory and visual modality (26/26 and 38/38) learned a 1Du strategy, whereas the vast majority in the spatial modality (35/41) were best fit by a 2D strategy.
evidence: This claim is supported by model fitting analysis of transfer data.

claim: Bayesian group model comparison confirmed that the frequency of 1D vs 2D models among non-random participants was similar between the auditory and visual modalities (BF=0.1).
source: Bayesian group model comparison confirmed that the frequency of 1D vs 2D models among non-random participants was similar between the auditory and visual modalities (BF=0.1, 'negative' evidence for a difference) but different between the auditory and spatial modalities (BF>100, 'decisive' evidence for a difference) and the visual and spatial modalities (BF>100; see Tables 6–9 for full results).
evidence: This claim is supported by Bayesian statistical analysis.

claim: Bayesian group model comparison confirmed that the frequency of 1D vs 2D models among non-random participants was different between the auditory and spatial modalities (BF>100).
source: Bayesian group model comparison confirmed that the frequency of 1D vs 2D models among non-random participants was similar between the auditory and visual modalities (BF=0.1, 'negative' evidence for a difference) but different between the auditory and spatial modalities (BF>100, 'decisive' evidence for a difference) and the visual and spatial modalities (BF>100; see Tables 6–9 for full results).
evidence: This claim is supported by Bayesian statistical analysis.

claim: Bayesian group model comparison confirmed that the frequency of 1D vs 2D models among non-random participants was different between the visual and spatial modalities (BF>100).
source: Bayesian group model comparison confirmed that the frequency of 1D vs 2D models among non-random participants was similar between the auditory and visual modalities (BF=0.1, 'negative' evidence for a difference) but different between the auditory and spatial modalities (BF>100, 'decisive' evidence for a difference) and the visual and spatial modalities (BF>100; see Tables 6–9 for full results).
evidence: This claim is supported by Bayesian statistical analysis.

claim: The use of a 1D strategy was much more likely than a 2D strategy when the manifold was defined by visual or auditory features.
source: This implies that the use of a 1D strategy (implying no rotational generalisation) was much more likely than a 2D strategy (implying rotational generalisation) when the manifold was defined by visual or auditory features (e.g. colour and shape or pitch and timbre), but the converse was true when the feature manifold was defined by coordinates in physical space (e.g. horizontal and vertical position).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the model comparison results.

claim: The use of a 2D strategy was much more likely than a 1D strategy when the feature manifold was defined by coordinates in physical space.
source: This implies that the use of a 1D strategy (implying no rotational generalisation) was much more likely than a 2D strategy (implying rotational generalisation) when the manifold was defined by visual or auditory features (e.g. colour and shape or pitch and timbre), but the converse was true when the feature manifold was defined by coordinates in physical space (e.g. horizontal and vertical position).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the model comparison results.

claim: For far transfer in Experiment 1, all non-random participants in the auditory modality (26/26) were best fit by a 1Du strategy.
source: For far transfer, the results were very similar. In the auditory modality, all non-random participants (26/26) were again best fit by a 1Du strategy, and in the visual modality, most (30/35) were fit by a 1Du strategy, 5/35 by a 1Ds strategy, and none by a 2D strategy (difference between auditory and visual, BF = 0.1).
evidence: This claim is supported by model fitting analysis of far transfer data.

claim: For far transfer in Experiment 1, most non-random participants in the visual modality (30/35) were fit by a 1Du strategy.
source: For far transfer, the results were very similar. In the auditory modality, all non-random participants (26/26) were again best fit by a 1Du strategy, and in the visual modality, most (30/35) were fit by a 1Du strategy, 5/35 by a 1Ds strategy, and none by a 2D strategy (difference between auditory and visual, BF = 0.1).
evidence: This claim is supported by model fitting analysis of far transfer data.

claim: For far transfer in Experiment 1, 5/35 non-random participants in the visual modality were fit by a 1Ds strategy.
source: For far transfer, the results were very similar. In the auditory modality, all non-random participants (26/26) were again best fit by a 1Du strategy, and in the visual modality, most (30/35) were fit by a 1Du strategy, 5/35 by a 1Ds strategy, and none by a 2D strategy (difference between auditory and visual, BF = 0.1).
evidence: This claim is supported by model fitting analysis of far transfer data.

claim: For far transfer in Experiment 1, no non-random participants in the visual modality were fit by a 2D strategy.
source: For far transfer, the results were very similar. In the auditory modality, all non-random participants (26/26) were again best fit by a 1Du strategy, and in the visual modality, most (30/35) were fit by a 1Du strategy, 5/35 by a 1Ds strategy, and none by a 2D strategy (difference between auditory and visual, BF = 0.1).
evidence: This claim is supported by model fitting analysis of far transfer data.

claim: For far transfer in Experiment 1, almost all non-random participants in the spatial modality (29/31) were best fit by a 2D strategy.
source: By contrast, in the spatial modality, where far transfer involved remapping from cardinal to polar coordinates or vice versa, almost all non-random participants (29/31) were again best fit by a 2D strategy (both BF>100 comparing with the auditory and visual modalities, 'decisive' evidence for a difference).
evidence: This claim is supported by model fitting analysis of far transfer data.

claim: When categories were characterised by temporal patterns in spatial location, participants learned to represent the 2D structure of the concept and generalised readily to rotated exemplars.
source: Together, these data show definitively that, when categories were characterised by temporal patterns in spatial location (e.g. where transitions in physical space were aligned with those on the feature manifold), participants learned to represent the 2D structure of the concept, and generalised readily to rotated (as well as translated) exemplars.
evidence: This is a summary inference drawn from the Experiment 1 results.

claim: When concepts were defined by patterns of nonspatial auditory or visual features, participants learned mappings to each category by relying on a single feature dimension and thus failed to form rotational invariant representations.
source: However, when concepts were defined by patterns of nonspatial auditory or visual features, participants learned mappings to each category by relying on a single feature dimension and thus failed to form rotational invariant representations.
evidence: This is a summary inference drawn from the Experiment 1 results.

claim: In Experiment 2, with spatial pre-training, 29/37 non-random participants were best fit by a 2D strategy when audition was the testing modality in the near transfer condition.
source: In the near transfer condition, with spatial pre-training, 29/37 non-random participants were best fit by a 2D strategy when audition was the testing modality, and 36/40 when vision was the testing modality.
evidence: This claim is supported by model fitting analysis of Experiment 2 data.

claim: In Experiment 2, with spatial pre-training, 36/40 non-random participants were best fit by a 2D strategy when vision was the testing modality in the near transfer condition.
source: In the near transfer condition, with spatial pre-training, 29/37 non-random participants were best fit by a 2D strategy when audition was the testing modality, and 36/40 when vision was the testing modality.
evidence: This claim is supported by model fitting analysis of Experiment 2 data.

claim: Participants who underwent visual (rather than spatial) pre-training failed to show a benefit when audition was the testing modality in Experiment 2.
source: By contrast, however, participants who underwent visual (rather than spatial) pre-training failed to show a benefit when audition was the testing modality. In fact, most (37/50) were best fit by the random model (see below), with 6/13 non-random participants favouring a 1Ds strategy.
evidence: This claim is supported by model fitting analysis of Experiment 2 data.

claim: In Experiment 2, most participants with visual pre-training (37/50) were best fit by the random model.
source: By contrast, however, participants who underwent visual (rather than spatial) pre-training failed to show a benefit when audition was the testing modality. In fact, most (37/50) were best fit by the random model (see below), with 6/13 non-random participants favouring a 1Ds strategy.
evidence: This claim is supported by model fitting analysis of Experiment 2 data.

claim: BFs exceeded 100, providing 'decisive' evidence that the 2D model was more favoured among the groups with spatial pre-training than that without in Experiment 2.
source: We once again calculated BF at the group level to assess the reliability of these results. We found that BFs exceeded 100, providing 'decisive' evidence that the 2D model was more favoured among the groups with spatial pre-training than that without.
evidence: This claim is supported by Bayesian statistical analysis.

claim: In the far transfer condition of Experiment 2, spatial pre-training allowed 29/38 participants in the auditory modality to successfully generalise via a 2D strategy.
source: Similarly, in the far transfer condition, spatial pre-training allowed 29/38 participants in the auditory modality and 13/16 participants in the visual modality to successfully generalise via a 2D strategy.
evidence: This claim is supported by model fitting analysis of far transfer data.

claim: In the far transfer condition of Experiment 2, spatial pre-training allowed 13/16 participants in the visual modality to successfully generalise via a 2D strategy.
source: Similarly, in the far transfer condition, spatial pre-training allowed 29/38 participants in the auditory modality and 13/16 participants in the visual modality to successfully generalise via a 2D strategy.
evidence: This claim is supported by model fitting analysis of far transfer data.

claim: Spatial pre-training provided an effective scaffold that allowed participants to learn auditory and visual objects in a 2D representational format that permitted generalisation to novel rotated exemplars.
source: In other words, spatial pre-training provided an effective scaffold that allowed participants to learn auditory and visual objects in a 2D representational format that permitted generalisation to novel rotated exemplars.
evidence: This is a summary inference drawn from the Experiment 2 results.

claim: Participants in Exp. 2c performed poorly during training and were more likely to be fit by the random models during transfer than those who performed the same auditory task in Exp. 1a.
source: Participants in Exp. 2c performed poorly during training and were more likely to be fit by the random models during transfer than those who performed the same auditory task in Exp. 1a.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of performance data between experiments.

claim: There is 'substantial' evidence in favour of a difference between Exp. 1a and Exp. 2c groups in near transfer (BF = 7.4).
source: Indeed, we computed the BF quantifying the relative likelihood of the random (R models) vs all other models (1D and 2D models) and found 'substantial' evidence in favour of a difference between groups both in near transfer (BF = 7.4) and in far transfer (BF = 2.7).
evidence: This claim is supported by Bayesian statistical analysis.

claim: Training with feedback on both 0° and 90° quadruplets effectively invalidates a 1D strategy.
source: In fact, this phenomenon makes sense, because training with feedback on both 0° and 90° quadruplets effectively invalidates a 1D strategy, because there no longer exists a unique mapping between categories and features in either of the two feature dimensions (note that training performance in Exp. 2c plateaus close to 50%).
evidence: This is an inference about why participants in Exp. 2c struggled, based on the task structure.

claim: The lack of a viable 1D strategy during training obliges participants to use a 2D strategy where possible.
source: This lack of a viable 1D strategy during training obliges participants to use a 2D strategy where possible.
evidence: This is an inference about participant strategy based on task constraints.

claim: In Experiment 3, non-random participants who enjoyed spatial pre-training were still prone to use a 2D strategy when audition was the testing modality (16/32 for near transfer and 17/31 for far transfer).
source: As predicted, non-random participants who enjoyed spatial pre-training were still prone to use a 2D strategy when audition was the testing modality (16/32 for near transfer and 17/31 for far transfer) as well as when vision was the testing modality (22/30 and 13/19), replicating the findings of Exp. 2.
evidence: This claim is supported by model fitting analysis of Experiment 3 data.

claim: In Experiment 3, non-random participants who enjoyed spatial pre-training were still prone to use a 2D strategy when vision was the testing modality (22/30 for near transfer and 13/19 for far transfer).
source: As predicted, non-random participants who enjoyed spatial pre-training were still prone to use a 2D strategy when audition was the testing modality (16/32 for near transfer and 17/31 for far transfer) as well as when vision was the testing modality (22/30 and 13/19), replicating the findings of Exp. 2.
evidence: This claim is supported by model fitting analysis of Experiment 3 data.

claim: Compared to Exp. 2, overall more participants relied on 1D strategies in Experiment 3.
source: However, compared to Exp. 2, overall more participants relied on 1D strategies.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of model fitting results between experiments.

claim: In the auditory modality in Exp. 3a, 16/32 were best fit by a 1D model in the near transfer condition.
source: In the auditory modality in Exp. 3a, 16/32 were best fit by a 1D model in the near transfer condition (9/32 1Du and 7/32 1Ds) and 14/31 in the far transfer condition (10/31 1Du and 4/31 1Ds).
evidence: This claim is supported by model fitting analysis of Experiment 3 data.

claim: Participants were more likely to be fit by a 1D model in Exp. 3a than Exp. 2a in the auditory modality (near transfer BF = 3.4 'substantial' evidence, far transfer BF = 1.5 'weak' evidence).
source: At the group level, the BF confirmed that participants were more likely to be fit by a 1D model in Exp. 3a than Exp. 2a in the auditory modality (frequency of 1D vs 2D models between Exp. 2a and Exp. 3a, near transfer BF = 3.4 'substantial' evidence, far transfer BF = 1.5 'weak' evidence).
evidence: This claim is supported by Bayesian statistical analysis comparing experiments.

claim: In the visual modality in Exp. 3b, 8/30 were best fit by a 1D model in the near transfer condition.
source: Similarly, in the visual modality in Exp. 3b, 8/30 were best fit by a 1D model in the near transfer condition (5/30 1Du and 3/30 1Ds) and 6/19 in the far transfer condition (6/19 1Du) (again, frequency of 1D vs 2D models between Exp. 2b and Exp. 3b, near transfer BF = 5.9 'substantial' evidence, far transfer BF = 2.2 'weak' evidence).
evidence: This claim is supported by model fitting analysis of Experiment 3 data.

claim: Participants who underwent nonspatial (visual) pre-training did not use a 2D strategy (1/30) but rather preferred 1D strategies in both near transfer (13/30 1Du and 16/30 1Ds) and far transfer conditions (10/28 1Du and 17/28 1Ds) in Experiment 3.
source: By contrast, participants who underwent nonspatial (visual) pre-training did not use a 2D strategy (1/30) but rather preferred 1D strategies in both near transfer (13/30 1Du and 16/30 1Ds) and far transfer conditions (10/28 1Du and 17/28 1Ds).
evidence: This claim is supported by model fitting analysis of Experiment 3 data.

claim: All BFs exceeded 100, providing 'decisive' evidence that the 2D model was more favoured among the groups with spatial pre-training than that without in Experiment 3.
source: Comparing these results with the frequency of 1D vs 2D models in conditions with spatial pre-training (Exp. 3a and 3b), we found that all BFs exceeded 100, providing 'decisive' evidence that the 2D model was more favoured among the groups with spatial pre-training than that without.
evidence: This claim is supported by Bayesian statistical analysis.

claim: Training exclusively on canonical (0°) quadruplets facilitates a 1D strategy, which is expressed more readily than in Exp. 2.
source: Thus, these results show that training exclusively on canonical (0°) quadruplets facilitates a 1D strategy, which is expressed more readily than in Exp. 2; but that the 2D strategy is still more likely for participants who underwent spatial pre-training.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing results between Experiments 2 and 3.

claim: The 2D strategy is still more likely for participants who underwent spatial pre-training in Experiment 3.
source: Thus, these results show that training exclusively on canonical (0°) quadruplets facilitates a 1D strategy, which is expressed more readily than in Exp. 2; but that the 2D strategy is still more likely for participants who underwent spatial pre-training.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the Experiment 3 results.

claim: Participants who did not experience spatial pre-training were still engaged in the task, but were not using the same strategy as the participants who experienced spatial pre-training (1D rather than 2D).
source: Further, the results show that participants who did not experience spatial pre-training were still engaged in the task, but were not using the same strategy as the participants who experienced spatial pre-training (1D rather than 2D).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing performance between conditions.

claim: The benefit of the spatial pre-training is not simply to increase the cognitive engagement of the participants.
source: Thus, the benefit of the spatial pre-training is not simply to increase the cognitive engagement of the participants.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the pattern of results showing different strategies rather than just different engagement levels.

claim: Spatial pre-training provides a scaffold to learn rotation-invariant representation of auditory and visual concepts even when rotation is never explicitly shown during pre-training.
source: Rather, spatial pre-training provides a scaffold to learn rotation-invariant representation of auditory and visual concepts even when rotation is never explicitly shown during pre-training.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the Experiment 3 results where pre-training only included canonical quadruplets.

claim: Participants are sensitive to the available strategies during pre-training, and use the 1D strategy when possible if they have not learned to associate features with space.
source: Furthermore, participants are sensitive to the available strategies during pre-training, and use the 1D strategy when possible if they have not learned to associate features with space.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the pattern of strategy use across experiments.

claim: 2Dness was powerfully predicted by training accuracy (Pearson correlation r2Dness,TRAINING = 0.80, p<0.001).
source: We found that 2Dness was powerfully predicted by training accuracy (Pearson correlation between 2Dness and training accuracy [r2Dness,TRAINING] = 0.80, p<0.001) in both Exp. 2 (r2Dness,TRAINING = 0.83, p<0.001) and Exp. 3 (r2Dness,TRAINING = 0.78, p<0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis of the data.

claim: The fact that training performance is highly correlated with 2Dness implies that participants who solved the training task formed representations that were generalisable in 2D.
source: The fact that training performance is highly correlated with 2Dness implies that participants who solved the training task formed representations that were generalisable in 2D; in other words, very few participants overfit to the training set.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the correlation analysis.

claim: Pre-training explained unique variance in 2Dness after accounting for mapping (r2Dness,PRETRAINING - MAPPING=0.17, p<0.01).
source: Pre-training did explain unique variance in 2Dness after accounting for mapping (correlation between pre-training and 2Dness after partialling out mapping [r2Dness,PRETRAINING - MAPPING]=0.17, p<0.01) and vice versa (r2Dness,MAPPING - PRETRAINING = 0.27, p<0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by partial correlation analysis.

claim: Mapping explained unique variance in 2Dness after accounting for pre-training (r2Dness,MAPPING - PRETRAINING = 0.27, p<0.001).
source: Pre-training did explain unique variance in 2Dness after accounting for mapping (correlation between pre-training and 2Dness after partialling out mapping [r2Dness,PRETRAINING - MAPPING]=0.17, p<0.01) and vice versa (r2Dness,MAPPING - PRETRAINING = 0.27, p<0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by partial correlation analysis.

claim: 2Dness was better predicted by mapping than by pre-training in Exp. 2a.
source: However, 2Dness was better predicted by mapping than by pre-training in Exp. 2a (r2Dness,MAPPING - PRETRAINING = 0.42, p<0.005 and r2Dness,PRETRAINING - MAPPING = 0.30, p<0.05), Exp. 2b (r2Dness,MAPPING - PRETRAINING = 0.41, p<0.005 and r2Dness,PRETRAINING - MAPPING = 0.04, p=0.81), Exp. 3a (r2Dness,MAPPING - PRETRAINING = 0.32, p<0.05 and r2Dness,PRETRAINING - MAPPING = 0.06, p=0.70) and Exp. 3b (r2Dness,MAPPING - PRETRAINING = 0.46, p<0.001 and r2Dness,PRETRAINING - MAPPING = 0.33, p<0.05).
evidence: This claim is supported by partial correlation analysis.

claim: The strong correlations between the mapping task performances and 2Dness suggest that learning the association between nonspatial and spatial features is the critical step that allows rotational generalisation.
source: The strong correlations between the mapping task performances and 2Dness suggest that learning the association between nonspatial and spatial features is the critical step that allows rotational generalisation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the correlation analysis results.

claim: Without spatial pre-training in Experiment 4, a sizeable proportion of participants still learned a 2D strategy in both the auditory (9/30 in near transfer, 9/28 in far transfer) and visual (12/19 and 7/19) modality.
source: Without spatial pre-training, a sizeable proportion of participants still learned a 2D strategy in both the auditory (9/30 in near transfer, 9/28 in far transfer) and visual (12/19 and 7/19) modality, although the majority relied on a 1D strategy (auditory modality: 4/30 1Du and 17/30 1Ds for near transfer, 4/38 1Du and 15/28 1Ds for far transfer; visual modality: 5/19 1Du and 6/19 1Ds for near transfer, 5/14 1Du and 2/14 1Ds for far transfer).
evidence: This claim is supported by model fitting analysis of Experiment 4 data.

claim: For ~20% participants in Experiment 4, the mere exposure to the mapping was sufficient to benefit from the spatial scaffolding effect and actually seeing the quadruplets in the spatial modality was not necessary for them.
source: Thus, for ~20% participants, the mere exposure to the mapping was sufficient to benefit from the spatial scaffolding effect and actually seeing the quadruplets in the spatial modality was not necessary for them.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the Experiment 4 results showing some 2D strategy use without spatial pre-training.

claim: Participants can generalise conceptual knowledge to novel sequences defined by rotations of stimulus feature transition vectors, but only if the features were themselves physical spatial locations or if nonspatial attributes had previously been mapped to a physical spatial location in a pre-training task.
source: We found that participants can generalise conceptual knowledge to novel sequences (quadruplets) defined by rotations of stimulus feature transition vectors, but only if the features were themselves physical spatial locations (e.g. x, y position; Exp. 1) or if nonspatial attributes had previously been mapped to a physical spatial location in a pre-training task (Exp. 2–4).
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings across all experiments.

claim: An explicit representation of physical space is a 'scaffold' that permits objects to be learned in a rotational-invariant fashion.
source: Thus, an explicit representation of physical space is a 'scaffold' that permits objects to be learned in a rotational-invariant fashion, and thus allows rotational generalisation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the overall pattern of results.

claim: The findings support the idea that neural representations of space form a critical substrate for learning abstractions in nonspatial domains.
source: This supports the idea that neural representations of space form a critical substrate for learning abstractions in nonspatial domains (Behrens et al., 2018; Bellmund et al., 2018; Summerfield et al., 2020; Gärdenfors, 2014).
evidence: This is an inference connecting the experimental findings to broader theory, with citations to relevant theoretical work.

claim: It is well known that humans learn rotational invariances for visual objects, whose features are organised in physical space.
source: It is well known that humans learn rotational invariances for visual objects, whose features are organised in physical space.
evidence: This is a statement about established knowledge in the field.

claim: An upside-down teapot can be recognised by the relative position of handle, lid, and spout.
source: For example, an upside-down teapot can be recognised by the relative position of handle, lid, and spout.
evidence: This is an example illustrating rotational invariance in object recognition.

claim: Participants generalised in different ways when the features in question were drawn from a nonspatial manifold, in either the visual or auditory domain.
source: However, we found it striking that participants generalised in such different ways when the features in question were drawn from a nonspatial manifold, in either the visual or auditory domain.
evidence: This is a summary observation from the experimental results.

claim: Participants had no trouble recognising patterns that were consistently translated in feature space in nonspatial conditions.
source: In these conditions, participants seemed to have no trouble recognising patterns that were consistently translated in feature space.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental results.

claim: Previous studies have shown that we can understand language in different accents, or name a familiar tune played at an atypical speed or pitch.
source: This is consistent with previous studies that have shown that we can understand language in different accents, or name a familiar tune played at an atypical speed or pitch (Dupoux and Green, 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Participants in nonspatial conditions used a representation that focused on just one of the two possible dimensions, and thus did not permit rotational generalisation.
source: However, they did so via a representation that focused on just one of the two possible dimensions, and thus did not permit rotational generalisation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the model fitting results.

claim: There was a clear dissociation between human ability to generalise patterns in physical space and a more abstract feature space.
source: There was thus a clear dissociation between human ability to generalise patterns in physical space and a more abstract feature space.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding from Experiment 1.

claim: Spatial pre-training allowed rotational generalisation even for sequences composed of nonspatial features.
source: Next, we showed that spatial pre-training allowed rotational generalisation even for sequences composed of nonspatial features.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding from Experiments 2 and 3.

claim: The neural representation of space may serve as a 'scaffold', allowing people to visualise and manipulate nonspatial concepts.
source: This implies that the neural representation of space may serve as a 'scaffold', allowing people to visualise and manipulate nonspatial concepts.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Around ~65% of the participants in Exp. 2c and Exp. 3c show a level of performance in the multimodal association task (>50%) which could only be achieved if they were attending to both dimensions.
source: Around ~65% of the participants show a level of performance in the multimodal association task (>50%) which could only be achieved if they were attending to both dimensions (performance attending to a single dimension would yield 25% and chance performance is at 6.25%).
evidence: This is an analysis of performance data to infer attentional strategy.

claim: Participants are attending to both dimensions even in the visual and auditory mapping case.
source: This suggests that participants are attending to both dimensions even in the visual and auditory mapping case.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the mapping task performance analysis.

claim: The findings are consistent with the more general idea that space is represented in an overlapping fashion with nonspatial information, such as time or number.
source: Rather, whilst we are not aware of previous studies that have tested spatial scaffolding in the way described here, our findings are consistent with the more general idea that space is represented in an overlapping fashion with nonspatial information, such as time or number (Dehaene et al., 2022).
evidence: This connects the findings to broader theoretical ideas, with citation.

claim: Sequences with regular spatial geometry are learned more readily than those composed of arbitrary patterns.
source: For example, sequences with regular spatial geometry are learned more readily than those composed of arbitrary patterns (Al Roumi et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Visuospatial skills are correlated with a variety of academic competences, especially in STEM subjects such as maths and engineering.
source: Our findings also cohere with evidence that visuospatial skills are correlated with a variety of academic competences, especially in STEM subjects such as maths and engineering (Stieff and Uttal, 2015), and that spatial training interventions (such as teaching mental rotation) in educational settings can improve nonspatial abilities, such as calculus grades (Sorby et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Spatial training interventions in educational settings can improve nonspatial abilities, such as calculus grades.
source: Our findings also cohere with evidence that visuospatial skills are correlated with a variety of academic competences, especially in STEM subjects such as maths and engineering (Stieff and Uttal, 2015), and that spatial training interventions (such as teaching mental rotation) in educational settings can improve nonspatial abilities, such as calculus grades (Sorby et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The idea that spatial representations form a generalised substrate for cognition draws on a long tradition in philosophy.
source: The idea that spatial representations form a generalised substrate for cognition – including for coding temporal structure – draws on a long tradition in philosophy (Kant, 2007), cognitive science (Gärdenfors, 2000), and neuroscience (Behrens et al., 2018; Bellmund et al., 2018; Summerfield et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to philosophical, cognitive science, and neuroscience work.

claim: The precise substrate for the spatial scaffolding effect is unclear.
source: The precise substrate for this effect is unclear, but it seems likely that neural assemblies activated by physical locations in space (e.g. in parietal or medial temporal lobe areas) are recycled for representing nonspatial patterns in data.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the neural mechanisms.

claim: It seems likely that neural assemblies activated by physical locations in space are recycled for representing nonspatial patterns in data.
source: The precise substrate for this effect is unclear, but it seems likely that neural assemblies activated by physical locations in space (e.g. in parietal or medial temporal lobe areas) are recycled for representing nonspatial patterns in data.
evidence: This is a speculative inference about neural mechanisms.

claim: The study does not provide a mechanistic model of the spatial scaffolding effect but rather delineates which aspects of the training are necessary for generalisation to happen.
source: We acknowledge that our study does not provide a mechanistic model of the spatial scaffolding effect but rather delineate which aspects of the training are necessary for generalisation to happen.
evidence: This is a statement about the scope and limitations of the study.

claim: The mapping task facilitates recycling of spatial neural assemblies by teaching participants a point-to-point mapping between nonspatial feature combinations and locations in physical space.
source: In our study, thus, the mapping task facilitates this recycling by teaching participants a point-to-point mapping between nonspatial feature combinations and locations in physical space.
evidence: This is an inference about the mechanism by which the mapping task works.

claim: Successfully learning mappings between spatial and nonspatial features was the strongest determinant of rotational generalisation.
source: Indeed, our correlation analysis and Exp. 4 suggested that successfully learning mappings between spatial and nonspatial features was the strongest determinant of rotational generalisation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the correlation analysis and Experiment 4 results.

claim: The mapping task was presented in an egocentric frame of reference defined by the x, y coordinates of the screen.
source: This mapping task was presented in an egocentric frame of reference defined by the x, y coordinates of the screen.
evidence: This describes a feature of the experimental design.

claim: Explicit representations of location in egocentric space in the primate are found in dorsal stream structures such as the posterior parietal cortex.
source: Explicit representations of location in egocentric space in the primate are found in dorsal stream structures such as the posterior parietal cortex (Colby et al., 1993).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to neuroscience literature.

claim: Current deep networks may be hampered by their failure to represent space explicitly.
source: Current deep networks – which successfully categorise lone objects in a natural image but often fail on tests of relational reasoning or scene understanding – may be hampered by their failure to represent space explicitly in this way (Summerfield et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a speculative claim about AI systems, with citation to prior work.

claim: All the effects observed in the experiments were consistent across near transfer conditions and far transfer conditions.
source: All the effects observed in our experiments were consistent across near transfer conditions (rotation of patterns within the same feature space), and far transfer conditions (rotation of patterns within a different feature space, where features are drawn from the same modality).
evidence: This is a summary observation about the consistency of results.

claim: The generality of spatial training for conceptual generalisation is shown by consistency across near and far transfer.
source: This shows the generality of spatial training for conceptual generalisation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the consistency of results across transfer conditions.

claim: An explicit representation of space might be the substrate for strong forms of transfer observed in humans.
source: This means that an explicit representation of space might be the substrate for strong forms of transfer observed in humans, such as when we understand the shared meaning between 'red, amber, green' at a traffic light and 'ready, set, go' before a race.
evidence: This is a speculative inference extending the findings to broader forms of transfer.

claim: The study did not test transfer across modalities nor transfer in a more natural setting.
source: We did not test transfer across modalities nor transfer in a more natural setting; we leave this for future studies.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations and scope of the study.

claim: In total, 558 participants were recruited with specific demographic characteristics.
source: In total, we collected data from 558 participants with the following demographic characteristics (see Table 1).
evidence: This describes the participant sample.

claim: Participants were recruited on the crowdsourcing platform Prolific.
source: Participants were recruited on the crowdsourcing platform Prolific (https://app.prolific.co/).
evidence: This describes the recruitment method.

claim: Participants received on average £10/hr for their time and effort, including a bonus on performance.
source: Participants received on average £10/hr for their time and effort, including a bonus on performance (£8.5/hr with random performances, £10.5/hr with perfect performances).
evidence: This describes the compensation structure.

claim: All experiments were approved by the Medical Sciences Research Ethics Committee of the University of Oxford (approval reference R50750/RE005).
source: All experiments were approved by the Medical Sciences Research Ethics Committee of the University of Oxford (approval reference R50750/RE005).
evidence: This describes the ethical approval for the study.

claim: The sample size was determined prior to the data collection, as indicated in the pre-registration documents.
source: The sample size was determined prior to the data collection, as indicated in the pre-registration documents.
evidence: This describes the study design process.
